transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*looks up from a workbench covered in wood shavings and brass fittings*

Good day to you, sir. I'm afraid the master builder is not here at present — he's away visiting suppliers in Venice and won't return for another three weeks at the earliest. 

*wipes hands on apron and approaches*

I am his senior journeyman. Perhaps I can be of assistance? Are you here regarding a commission, or is this about an existing instrument?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Yes, I'd like to discuss an existing instrument. I believe it was a custom-built fortepiano that was delivered to the Imperial Court's music room a little over a year ago. It appears to be in rather rough condition.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*frowns slightly and crosses arms*

A fortepiano for the Imperial Court, you say? Yes, I recall that commission — a fine instrument, one of the master's best works. Walnut case with ivory keys, if memory serves.

*walks over to a ledger on a side table and flips through pages*

Delivered fourteen months ago... signed for by the Court's own servants upon delivery and acceptance. The master was quite proud of that piece.

What sort of "rough condition" are we discussing here? That instrument was in perfect order when it left this workshop, I can assure you of that. The master inspected every detail himself before delivery.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Well, there are several problems. Some of the keys stick, the pedal mechanism seems to be faulty, and the tone in the upper register is thin and tinny. I brought it to the attention of the court's musicians, but they were unable to identify the issue. I'm afraid it has become quite a burden for everyone involved.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*straightens up and shakes head firmly*

Sir, I understand your concerns, but you must appreciate the position we're in. That instrument was delivered over a year ago — fourteen months, to be precise. Much can happen to a fortepiano in that time, especially in a court music room where who knows how many hands have played it, in what conditions of humidity and temperature.

*taps the ledger meaningfully*

All commissions from this workshop are considered fulfilled upon delivery and acceptance. The Court's own servants signed the receipt — it's right here in our records. Our guild rules forbid reopening a completed commission without the master's personal approval, and as I've said, he won't be back for weeks.

*softens tone slightly but remains firm*

Even if the master were here, after fourteen months of use, any repairs would be considered new work, not warranty obligations. Sticking keys, pedal issues — these are matters of maintenance and care, not craftsmanship defects that would have been apparent at delivery.

If this were a matter of days or even weeks after delivery, it would be different. But over a year? I'm afraid my hands are tied, sir.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: I understand your position, but this is not just a matter of maintenance and care. The instrument is not meeting the necessary standards of sound quality. We need it to be fixed promptly, as it is causing significant issues for the musicians. I understand that the master builder is currently away, but I hope you can find a way to prioritize this repair and ensure that it is completed as soon as possible.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*sets jaw firmly and meets your gaze*

Sir, with all due respect, you're not hearing me. This is not about prioritization or urgency — it's about guild regulations and the terms under which we conduct business.

*gestures toward the workshop*

I am a journeyman, not the master. I do not have the authority to reopen a completed, accepted, and paid commission. The guild is quite strict about this — if I were to take it upon myself to begin work on an instrument the master considers delivered and final, I could face discipline, and the workshop could lose its standing.

*leans against the workbench*

The Court accepted that instrument in perfect working order fourteen months ago. Whatever has befallen it since — whether through heavy use, environmental conditions, or simple wear — falls outside the original commission. You speak of "sound quality standards," but whose standards are we discussing after more than a year of use?

If you wish to have the instrument repaired, I can note your request in our ledger, and when the master returns in three weeks' time, he can decide whether to accept it as *new work* — for which there would naturally be a fee assessed.

But I will not — I *cannot* — simply agree to repair or replace it as though the original commission were somehow incomplete. That matter was settled and signed for long ago.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: I appreciate your position as a journeyman, and I understand the rules and regulations governing this type of situation. However, I must insist that you find a way to address the issues with the fortepiano. The musicians have been struggling with it, and it is causing significant problems for their performances. I understand that it may be beyond the scope of the original commission, but the sound quality needs to be improved. Can you please find a solution within your capacity as a journeyman?

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*exhales slowly, maintaining polite but unyielding demeanor*

Sir, I fear we are going in circles. You keep saying you "understand" my position, yet you continue to insist I do precisely what I've explained I cannot do.

*spreads hands*

My capacity as a journeyman is to maintain the workshop in the master's absence, handle routine inquiries, and accept commissions for his consideration upon return. It does *not* extend to making exceptions to guild rules or contractual terms, no matter how urgent the Court's needs may be.

*pauses, then speaks more carefully*

I wonder — are you here in an official capacity on behalf of the Imperial Court? Because if the Court itself has a complaint about work delivered to them, that would be a matter for formal correspondence between the Court administrators and the master builder directly. It would need to go through proper channels.

*gestures toward the door*

As it stands, all I can offer is this: I will make a detailed note of your concerns in our records. When the master returns, I will ensure he is informed immediately. If he judges the matter warrants his attention, he may choose to inspect the instrument himself or propose terms for repair work.

But I will not — I truly *cannot* — commit this workshop to action without his authorization. That is my final word on the matter, sir.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: I understand your position, but I implore you to reconsider. The musicians need this instrument to be fixed. The sound quality is crucial for their performances. I appreciate the regulations and procedures, but in this particular case, I believe it is important to prioritize the needs of the musicians. Please find a way to accommodate this request within your duties as a journeyman.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:

Sir, I have explained our position three times now, clearly and completely. You continue to ask me to "reconsider" and "find a way" as though repetition will somehow change guild law or the terms of a completed commission.

*steps back from the workbench, posture becoming more formal*

I am not unsympathetic to the musicians' difficulties, but their needs do not override the regulations that govern this workshop and my employment within it. You speak of priorities — my priority is to maintain the integrity and reputation of this establishment, which means adhering to the rules that protect both craftsman and client.

*voice firm but measured*

I have offered you what I can: to record your complaint and ensure the master addresses it upon his return in three weeks. That is the extent of my authority and the extent of what I will do.

If the Court requires more immediate action, I suggest you consult other instrument makers in the city who might be willing to assess and repair the fortepiano under their own names. But this workshop will not reopen a commission that was completed and accepted fourteen months ago without the master builder's personal authorization.

*crosses arms definitively*

Now, sir — do you wish me to make that notation in our ledger, or have you other business here?
